And then I'm going to skip down to another line: "Arkan's guards brought another man. I believe that he was the owner of a cafe called Saran in Erdut Bijeljina," as it is typed here, which I'm going to suggest is Erdut Planina, "he was short, slightly overweight. He spoke in a local Hungarian dialect. He was wearing a green jumper with a certain pattern. He was about 40 to 50 years old. They started interrogating him, and when he replied that he didn't know the answer, Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, kicked him in the genitals and then the man fell on the ground." And this continues onto the next page of the English transcript. I'm going to skip down about six or seven lines. It goes on to describe what was happening to this person. And then what's read to you is: "I only recall the names Sabonja or Saboto and Ivan or Josip Pap which I saw identification papers for the persons brought in. They were all" -- sorry, "there were all Croatian Hungarians from Erdut and Erdut Bijeljina," which, again, I would suggest is Planina, "there must have been 15 or 20 of them detained in the prison which made the prison full." Now continuing down some more, finally, at the end there,

utterances.speaker: MR. DZURO SAYS
utterances.text: "So it continues. I was going to read further about the activities of the SNB. Do you want to comment so far?" And what you said is: "I can only say that I know nothing about this and what I think of Puki I told you already about this Stricevic." Now, Mr. Hadzic, this is your suspect in 2002, and recognising your claim that you didn't know the family name Pap but that you only knew nicknames. What we do know here is that Mr. Dzuro read to you a witness statement that referred to the arrest, detention and beating of Hungarians from Erdut Planina, the Planina. It refers to the restaurant Saran. Same restaurant you referred to in your testimony in this trial.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we called that restaurant Kod Ferike.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, finally, Mr. Dzuro read the name -- he mentioned the name of Sabonja from the statement which also is one of the nicknames you knew from one of the Pap family members. You mentioned -- you mentioned that in your direct evidence in this case when you were describing the Pap family. You knew about the brother, nicknamed Sabonja. You knew they were Hungarians from the Planina. You knew they had a restaurant. You knew the restaurant was called Saran. And all of these things were mentioned to you in your suspect interview, and yet at the time you claimed that you knew nothing about this. So I'm going to suggest, Mr. Hadzic, that in fact in your suspect interview you did know about these people. You just didn't want to admit and you were seeking to distance yourself from them. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true. You got things confused here. If you allow me to correct you? Sobonja, that's a completely different person. He is the brother of a lady witness who testified here and he came to a tragic end. I heard that. I cannot remember his real name and surname now. He has nothing to do with the Pap family. That's not his last name. As for the restaurant, Saran I only realised later that that was its name. We called it Kod Ferike and Ferike is the old man who was beaten here. That was the description. And he had two sons. One was also called Ferike, and the other one was Mihajlan [phoen]. We called him Misi. I did not know the name of their mother. That's the only name I didn't know so I addressed her as madam, and I knew that their last name was Pap, and they were my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I'm going to put it to you that Mr. Dzuro provided you with an ample amount of information to link the people he is referring to, the incident he is referring to, to what you knew of the Pap family, suggesting that you were not candid with him, you knew more than you told him at the time, and to this day you knew more than you're telling us as well. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't even know what I said to him, what he asked me about, expect for this bit that you read to me about Stricevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic also asked you to comment on the incident that is addressed in paragraph 9 of the indictment in this case, which is the incident involving the people who had been arrested by Arkan in Klisa and brought to Erdut to the training centre there. And I want to here again compare your evidence, your comment about that in this case to what you said to Mr. Dzuro in your suspect interview. Now, this is the 14th of July, in this case, transcript 9737. And Mr. Zivanovic actually referred -- he said: "Do you know anything about the arrests of these people from Klisa? Do you know anything about the incident? What you can tell us? And you said: "I'll tell you all I know about this incident, but it was only ten years later that I really learned what happened. I heard the details only here in The Hague during the witness evidence. Towards the end of 1991, on the 11th of November, 1991, I came from Novi Sad to Erdut in the morning. The driver told me three men who were standing to the side were looking for me, looking for a fourth man, who was not from Klisa unlike the first three. Among them was a man whom they knew. He worked as a car mechanic in Erdut. Those three men, I knew them. I knew they were from Klisa. I played football with them. They asked me if I was able to assist them because they had a report that some people who had been in the fields doing their farm work, as I thought then, had been arrested." Again, this is your evidence from last month: "Later I learned that they were actually arrested and some were near their workplace, and these men also said that this could have been done by Arkan's Men and I said -- I thought, in fact, that they were not able to go there where Arkan's Men were based." And then you go on to describe -- not going to go all through it. But you say: "There was only 100 yards to the gate of their base, and I said, Wait for me. I'll go there. I literally ran to that gate along with my escort, and when I came to the gate I saw Arkan. I asked him if he knew anything about any arrests in Klisa, if he had any information at all. He seemed very nervous and upset which I couldn't understand at the time. He said, Why does everyone blame me for everything? I am not the police. I have nothing to do with arrests." I'm going to skip down in your testimony to talk more about your conversation with Arkan. And then you say: "And then he," Arkan, "asked, Who told you this." And you said: "But I realised those men would be in trouble if I told them who they were -- if I told him who they were. So I just left there. I said" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down for the sake of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Apologies: "But I realised those men would be in trouble if I told him who they were, so I just left there. I said, Okay, if you don't know anything. And I left. I went back to those three men and told him those people were not in Arkan's base. One of them was called Ormaz and another was called Rajko." And then you went on to talk, Mr. Hadzic, in your direct testimony, if you recall, you described how your wife went to try to find some of these people, to talk to them about that incident. Do you remember describing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in your evidence you said: "Anyway, I told those men what I found out and went towards that place where the government seat was. And then I saw Djordje Djukovic, who was a friend of mine also from Klisa, and I said in passing, Those people are not held by Arkan. And forgot one more thing. Arkan said to me, Why are you looking for them. They are Ustashas. They must have defected to the Croatian side." And then you continue. You said: "And I told Cukovic that those people were not held by Arkan because I knew he was from Klisa. Then I went into my office where some people were waiting to have a meeting with me, went out from the canteen came Mica Panisic, who was the manager of an enterprise called Dalj." And then goes on to describe your encounter with him. You said: "He was talking and making a racket. I didn't even know he was manager of those people because I didn't make the connection." So, Mr. Hadzic, that's a pretty full account of your awareness or your involvement, if I can put it that way, with the inquiry that was made after these people from Klisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now if we could please have 65 ter 4974.08D. This is tab 1089 Mr. President. And going to page 8 there of the English transcript. Now, again, in the suspect interview -- and if we could please -- well, we can actually broadcast this, Mr. President, because Mr. Dzuro is actually reading this same incident as it's alleged in the Slobodan Milosevic indictment which was a public document. And he says: "I will now look into the indictment of Slobodan Milosevic versus the Prosecutor for crimes in Croatia." And then he refers to the 11th of November, 1991, the same day you just -- you just -- your testimony: "Members of the TO SAO SBWS under the command of Zeljko Raznjatovic arrested seven non-Serbs, civilians in the village of Klisa." So he just goes on to describe the detainees from Klisa, two of them were released; five of them held, interrogated, killed, and buried. And then he says: "Do you know anything about the case where the people were arrested were employed by IPK Dalj were arrested and taken to the training centre in Dalj, in Erdut, sorry, in Erdut." And you say: "No, I know nothing about that." Mr. Hadzic, that's quite a stark contrast from the rather detailed account you've given this Trial Chamber about your efforts to find out about these Klisa people. Why didn't you give that account to Mr. Dzuro? Why didn't you tell him about it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when he put that question to me that way I really didn't know at that time that those people from were IPK Dalj, that they were in fact from Klisa. What I knew about them was that they had been digging somewhere in Klisa - I didn't know that they were employed somewhere - and together with them they defected to the Croatian side. I thought maybe that this was some other group. I didn't know they were killed. I only heard (redacted) (redacted) happened and then I made the connections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this goes on and we should not broadcast, Mr. President, what's -- what's now -- we see on the page - I apologise - is part of a statement that I think should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if we could just for a moment move into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So here we are in your suspect interview, Mr. Hadzic. Mr. Dzuro is reading you the statement of a person, a witness. And what he is reading to you from the statement, here we see in the third line says: "I decided to go with Djordje Cukovic from Klisa to Erdut to [sic] make some inquiries." And so then the statement goes on to talk about that. They walked in the cabinet. And then moving to the next page, page 10, again the statement says: "Having left the office we walked through the hall where we met with Goran Hadzic. He was coming in with some people. Djordje Cukovic explained to Goran Hadzic that the family members of the missing from Klisa were coming to his home and asked [sic] him what had happened to them."

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the next page in my version. I don't see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hadzic, in your direct testimony in this case after describing what you did for those three men, three or four men from Klisa who had come and met you at the gate after you went over to ask Arkan what have become of these people from Klisa, and your testimony in this case you go on to talk about encountering Mr. Cukovic and another person or the same question or very similar question comes up and that is the fate of some people from Klisa. Mr. Dzuro is asking you very significantly similar about -- he is providing you with very similar information, asking you to comment on this. And yet as we see at the bottom of page 10, you claimed: "I don't remember that event. I don't even know how they addressed me. I don't know ... I quite certainly didn't realise that they were missing. If I had known, I quite certainly would have tried to do something about it [sic]." Now, the fact is, Mr. Hadzic, that these very significant discrepancies, difference between what you said to Mr. Dzuro in 2002 and what you've told this Trial Chamber, really can't be reconciled. And the fact is that this evidence, this -- this story you've come up with now about trying to go inquire with Arkan is just a fabrication, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, I have to explain this. Since we are in open session, I will not be mentioning names, but what was read from the statement to me is simply not true. That witness simply made up something and mixed things up and I couldn't recognise the story. I had seen him only for ten seconds. I couldn't connects the dots. What radio station? What story? I never heard anyone mention the radio station. I thought it was a made-up story. Here during my testimony only I understood what story that was. What it was about. And what people it concerned. I didn't even know that those people had been killed, those that I made inquiries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we briefly pass into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What we see here on page 13, Mr. Hadzic, after Mr. Dzuro is asking you to comment on the names of victims, and here you said that you didn't know them by their family name, maybe nicknames. Then again, paragraph 54 which is from the Milosevic indictment, this is what you said: "This is what we talked about just a while ago in connection with Klisa; right? Everything that I said -- I knew I already said. I don't know anything further than that." So, Mr. Hadzic, you had, in fact, made the connection with Klisa, to the missing people from Klisa that you were being asked about, and at that time, despite what you've said in this trial, at that time you claimed you didn't know anything about it. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true. I didn't connect the fact that those were one and the same people. I didn't know that the workers from Klisa were employed in Dalj. I didn't connect these two things. The distance runs in kilometres. I didn't realise it was one and the same company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That would be all for -- on this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before we start, I'd like just to -- to let you know that the question from the Prosecution, on the page 59, line 51 [sic] through page 60, line 6, are misrepresented, because the Prosecution failed to quote the two-page -- on two page before on the screen that Mr. Dzuro, investigator of the Prosecution, gave to the witness the indictment from Milosevic, and all those names were read from this -- that indictment. Sorry. However, we'll -- we'll clarify it in our re-direct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, during your direct examination at transcript page 9673 by your counsel, Mr. Zivanovic, asked you, did you know that during 1991 there was some exchange of prisoners in the territory of SBWS. And you said: "I do know that." And he asked: "Can you tell us how it came about? And you said: "I was not personally involved, but I found out from Ilija Koncarevic about it and also through the media. There was also a delegation that visited us from SFRY. It was they who organised these prisoner exchanges." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in our parts of your evidence, your direct examination, you asserted that the prisoner exchanges were exclusively within the authority of the JNA. Is that also your position?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You said at transcript page 9676: "It was all decided by federal institutions." Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the best of my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit P3119, which is tab -- sorry, Mr. President. We don't have a tab number for this one. This was added after the direct evidence, or the direct examination, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this is from the 6th of August, 1991, Mr. Hadzic, report on the activities of the commission for implementing the decision of the SFRY Presidency on immediate absolute cease-fire. Do you remember this commission, Mr. Hadzic? Do you remember the work of this in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now, I can't remember. Maybe if you could show me something it could jog my memory. But right now I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: On page 5 of the English version. And the B/C/S, it's under the heading Roman numeral III, this sets out the membership of the commission, the commission's working group, I should say, consisting of the people we see here. Tupurkosvski, Bogicevic, the names continue, representatives of Serbian people eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem with the participation of Goran Hadzic, Ilija Koncarevic, Vitomir Devetak, Knezevic, Bogic, Petrovic. Does this help you remember, Mr. Hadzic, that you were involved in this commission in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in its work. We had that meeting. I remember Vasil Tupurkovski and Bogic Bogicevic had come from Belgrade. I don't remember Gracanin and the other person. We had some meeting in Vajska but we were not members of that commission. We were not part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall that this commission also dealt with the issue of prisoner exchange?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I recall, it was at the level of the Presidency of the SFRY. They decided about it. I don't know what the commission was doing. I was not a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we at least agree that either you or members of your government, or, I should say what was to be the government of the SBWS in August of 1991, were actually participating or were involved in the issues regarding prisoner exchange?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody from the government was there, only Ilija Koncarevic, but he was not there as a representative of the government. He was there because he had some connections with people from Belgrade and later he was in the assembly, but he did not come from the government. Even today I don't know what kind of contact he had with them, but he was not there as a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1717 -- apologies. No, it's not tab 1717.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yeah. This is a FBIS document, Mr. President, 1D03021.1. We've made a redacted version of it because the FBIS documents have that confidentiality issue, and so this is a -- this would be a public redacted version of what's already in evidence as D134 which is the document at tab 1717.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is a news report, Mr. Hadzic, "Tanjug," Belgrade. And again, this is 8th of August, 1991, meeting of the SFRY Presidency's Commission on Cease-fire, and it names the people whose names we just saw in the previous document, at least some of them. Koncarevic and Petrovic here are named as the representatives. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that in English. But I don't really understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's my -- my question is simply whether these two gentlemen -- would you agree these two gentlemen were involved in the issue of this commission -- the issues of this commission?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I know Ilija Koncarevic was involved with exchanges, and he made lists of Serbs who had remained on the Croatian side, Serbs who were supposed to be exchanged. But I didn't understand that he had formally been appointed to that job.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And moving down to paragraph 4 of this document, makes reference to members of the commission, et cetera, "will visit tomorrow 9th of August, the villages of Dalj and Sarvas to solve the pressing problems in these villages."

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- do you recall that visit? Do you recall the event that's referred to there, 9th of August?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember now. I don't remember this specific date. I believe Tupurkovski visited Dalj once more, but I don't know on which date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And part of what they were doing was dealing with the issue of prisoners, lists of individuals and prisoners and exchanges. Isn't that, at least in part, what this was about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't give evidence about it. I see as much as you do from -- from this. But I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's move to one -- sorry. I want to go to your testimony, Mr. Hadzic, in this case. Transcript page 9676. You were being asked by your counsel about your attendance at one meeting at Borovo Selo of this working group from the Presidency. You were there alongside Koncarevic, Petrovic, Kojic. You said, yes, you remember it because Drazen Budisa and Zivko Milosevic were also there. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember when Drazen Budisa and Zivko Jusbasic were there, not Milosevic as I heard in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at page 9676 of the transcript, and according to that, you did mention Mr. Zivko Milosevic there at the time of your direct exam.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a mistake. It's Zivko Jusbasic who was on some Croatian delegation. He was an ethnic Serb but he was part of the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 920 which is Exhibit P2988.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this is a report, Mr. Hadzic, this is from the Zagreb radio Croatia network but it does refer to an exchange of prisoners and the participation of various people that we've just been talking about beginning in paragraph 2. It's a recording of Mr. Tupurkovski. Refers to a visit to Borovo Selo; talks on the implementation on the decision of cease-fire. Now, do you remember that meeting? Is this the meeting I was just asking you about from your testimony in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the meeting where the cease-fire was discussed. I do not remember having the exchange of prisoners discussed. It says here Zivko Jusbasic as I have testified, not Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hadzic at page 9676 of your testimony on direct examination, Mr. Zivanovic was asking you about one meeting at Borovo Selo of this working group, and you said you were there. And he asked you is it true that this all-for-all prisoner exchange referred to in paragraph 1 - we can go to that document - took place? And you said, "Yes, it's true. Actually, and then you went on to correct that it should be Jusko. You corrected the name. Does that refresh your memory from your earlier testimony that -- that you agree that there was an all-for-all prisoner exchange that was part of the discussions at this Borovo Selo meeting that you attended.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that that exchange was all for all. There's no denying that. But I don't remember that we made any decisions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 920 which is Exhibit 2988. Sorry. That's the one we just had. Tab 1700. 65 ter 4809.22. This is a video-clip. And the interpreters should have this in the booths, so we'll wait to hear that they've got it handy. 65 ter 4809.22.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We've got. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "That would be the condition for further negotiations. Would that be an all-for-all -- on an all-for-all basis or not? "Goran Hadzic: Only on an all-for-all basis. That has been agreed before. At the beginning of our conversation, Mr. Budisa stressed that he did not recognise the national council and said that we were only representatives of our people. We replied that we also did not recognise the government of Croatia and that we participate in negotiations as representatives of the Serbian and Croatian people, that we do not negotiate with the government of Croatia. That is how we reached the agreement."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadzic, does that clip relate to your involvement in the prisoner exchange, the all-for-all prisoner exchange, in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it does, now that I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3233, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you remember that the SBWS TO led by Ilija Koncarevic with the assistance of Milan Martic and units under his command captured the town of Bilje at the beginning of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Ilija Koncarevic was never a member of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. But I don't know. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's my mistake. I meant to say Ilija Kojic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also this is the first time I hear that Ilija Kojic took part in these operations in Baranja. What I knew was that this was done by the JNA, that unit from Sombor. That they took part in that conflict. That's what I heard about from these people in Baranja. I hadn't known anything about it. I think that Martic certainly had not been there. Had he been there, I would have to hear about it from someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 103, 65 ter 4869.3. And this is also video footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic. Sorry, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't know whether the year is correct in line 11. Page 67, line 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that. Maybe I misspoke there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I'm asking you if you knew about an operation resulting in the -- the capture or the liberation of Bilje in September, early September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My understanding was that you were referring to 1991, so I didn't even notice 1993. It's only later that I heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So this video-clip here that we're about to look at, 65 ter 4869.3, if the interpreters have it, we can play that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Last night soldiers from the so-called Croatian National Guard Corps pounded the Trepelje [phoen] neighbourhood of Borovo Selo. Mortars positioned in Borovo Naselje and Vukovar. As a result, six defenders were wounded, two of them seriously. They were immediately taken to Vajska on the opposite bank of the Danube. There was no panic amongst the defenders. There was panic though among members of the guard corps and the MUP in Bilje and on the positions around Osijek where Martic's Kninjas crushed them and captured some 30 combatants of Tudjman's. They are now in police custody of the Autonomous District in Borovo Selo and are being questioned. Early this morning the village of Palaca came under mortar and small-arms attacks in which about 30 defenders of the villages of Palaca and Markusica who came to their aid were wounded. The wounded fighters have told us about casualties of these attacks. Tudjman's combatants have also been attacking the village of Brsadin trying to capture it at any cost. Brsadin is an extremely important strategic point on the Vukovar-Vinkovci Road. The government of the Autonomous Region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem met in its Dalj headquarters today to specify the ministry's duties in this difficult period. It is definitely the biggest news that officials of the Autonomous Region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and SAO of Krajina have been invited to a meeting of ministers that is to be head in The Hague on the 7th of September. On this occasion, Prime Minister Hadzic told Belgrade television as follows. "Goran Hadzic: We have been invited. I have not received the official invitation yet but the foreign minister has told me over the phone that we might go to The Hague on Saturday and this would be the final formal recognition even though we have already been recognised, only this would be the formal recognition of the world public."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, does this help you remember the Bilje operation and the capture of about 30 Croatian fighters in early September 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't really help me. I don't remember that I knew anything about these operations at the time when they were taking place. It's only later that I heard that Bilje was free and that one could go there. But it wasn't my understanding that Martic had taken part in that. At that time I didn't know that. This is the first time I see this report on TV. And I don't think this was a government meeting. As far as I managed to see the faces very quickly, I saw only myself and Kojic, as far as the government is concerned, and the others I managed to catch a glimpse of, they are neighbours, friends, not members of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It refers to the announcement that you would be going to The Hague on I think the following day or within a day or two on the 7th of September. Are you able to comment on that part of the video and indicate whether that is an accurate statement of -- an accurate reflection of what was happening in respect of The Hague?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Caslav Otic said that to me that we would be invited to go to The Hague. But later on I heard that Babic had refused so we couldn't go either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In any event, this happened in early September, then, this possibility of going to The Hague and its connection to the government meeting or the reference to the government meeting that we just saw?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. It wasn't discussed at that meeting. I mean, going to The Hague. In my view, these three things have nothing do with one another. Prisoners, the government session, this interview of mine; these are three completely different things. This journalist made this compilation. But I remember that at that time Mr. Henry Wijnaendts came to Borovo Selo and Mr. Ahrens somehow around the 6th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's right. And that's what we're going to talk about in just a minute or two. You've referred to Mr. Ahrens' testimony. And for the record, this is at 7678 to 7680 of the transcript. He talked about coming to Boro on the 6th of September, meeting with you. And do you recall his testimony about what he and his colleague saw during a break in the negotiations when they went down and they were able to see prisoners behind a grated window from a table. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he talked about that but I didn't understand that that could be seen from the table where we were. He said that he saw that when he went out of the building to take walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1032 which is P244 P244. This is another video, so we'll wait for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please have the 65 ter number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We've found it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Reporter: Despite fears, clashes between the defender and the Ustashai soldiers, the territorial districts of the Autonomous District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem are fully in control of the situation. Martic's Kninjas have captured Bilje, a strategically important point in the vicinity of Osijek and broke up Tudjman's formations. We spoke to Ilija Kojic, commander of the Territorial Defence, and Milan Martic, secretary of the Krajina MUP, about the situation in this part of Slavonia and the claims of the Croatian television that Martic has brought tanks into Borovo Selo. "Ilija Kojic: Well, the current situation is difficult because they are not observing the truces. This was evident last night when over 50 mortar and cannon shells landed in Borovo Selo. They continued targeting Belo Brdo throughout the night and this morning. Fighting has been going on since this morning at Palaca and Silas. There are many wounded but no dead so far. We shall see later how the situation develops. "Reporter: What do you think is the key to this problem, so to speak? "Ilija Kojic: Well, essentially the problem is that they do not observe anything. They disregard everything and show no represent for rules, agreements, or anything. They just do as they please and they act accordingly. "Milan Martic: Well, the tanks belong to the Yugoslav People's Army and it is well known that we and the army have a common goal. It is true that we have brought Kninja special troops here and the results are already obvious. Bilje has been liberated and some 30 guardsmen have been arrested. They are here. I believe that the effects of the Kninjas' performance are evident and that they played a significant role in this whole operation. "Reporter: That Martic's fighters mean business has been demonstrated by the fact that some 30 members of the MUP are imprisoned in Borovo Selo after having been captured in the clashes yesterday. "A male voice: I was captured in Bilje. When we were attacked we surrendered. I was in the reserve forces of the guard corps. We were assigned to defend the village. We were guarding the village."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadzic, we've seen two video-clips here that talk about the operation at Bilje in September, the capture of 30 Croat prisoners, Martic and his Kninjas there. Kojic is talking about it. There are references to over 50 mortar and cannon shells landing in Borovo Selo. You must remember this, Mr. Hadzic. You do remember this, don't you, these events in early September?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I do not remember. At that time nobody had told me about this. Otherwise, too, the polices never gave me any reports, not even when I was president of the republic. And then also they probably thought that I was not a reliable enough to receive reports especially about these military matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we have just seen footage of you in the government meeting with Mr. Kojic there. So where were you then? I mean, you were either in Dalj or Borovo, Mr. Hadzic. I mean, how could you not know about all of these events? Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need for you to apologise. I think that a picture was taken of me in Dalj and this journalist in the white shirt -- I didn't recognise the journalist. These were not members of the government. These were people who stopped by to chat with me in Dalj. I recognised one of my neighbours. I'm not even sure of the time-frame, when this took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. I want to just replay a little bit of this footage from -- if we could start it from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you able to read the name that we see there, Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, these are the prisoners, captured prisoners, who were being held in Borovo Selo at the time that you met with Ambassador Ahrens there. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ahrens testified about that. He said that he saw them when he got out of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know this man who is identified as Zeljko Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the last name I read was Filipovic. The name was Zeljko Filipovic. Yes, it is typed up properly here. No, I didn't know anybody from Bilje. I didn't know any Serbs or Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1134, P118.111.11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Confidential one, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is the public redacted version, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We've looked at this document a few times, Mr. Hadzic. These are the group of prisoners involved in the incident on the 21st of September, 1991. And among the names of those people who were referred to as having been led out by Arkan, we see a name Zeljko Filipcoc. What's going to indicate here -- I'm going to suggest to you that it's Mr. Filipovic, the gentleman we just saw in the video who was being held in Borovo in early September, just a few weeks earlier. Do you know how he came from Borovo Selo to Dalj?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I read over there was Zeljko Filipovic. I don't know whether it's that person. I just know that there was this exchange, all-for-all, and I really don't know if anybody stayed behind. I really don't know?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall the testimony of Witness GH-003?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the record, it's our submission that the person indicated or shown in the video talking, the prisoner is one of those scheduled as a victim in regard to paragraph 24 of the indictment. Flipcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I saw some differences -- differences in last name of this person. As far as I recall it on the video, there was a last name Filipsic and here is Filicic and the witness read Filipovic. So I see there are differences, I think, in the last name. Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think we all saw that, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we agree. I think it's pretty obvious, actually, that there are differences in the witness's name as shown on the television versus the name as it is set out in the exhibit, the report that we were just looking at. So we do concede that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, during your direct examination, you were asked some questions about how you saw your authority and your powers during the time that you were president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and I've got some follow-up on that. On page 9838, on the 15th of July, counsel, Mr. Zivanovic, asked you: "How do understand this particular responsibility?" And here he is referring to Article 78 of the constitution of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and we're going to look at that in a few minutes, particularly in regard to the authority under the constitution that the president controls armed forces in peace and war and people's resistance in war time, and we'll talk more about this in a moment, but what your answer was -- at that time was to say: "I should only like to say that this constitution of 19 December, 1991, was adopted when Milan Babic was president, and in gest, my friends and I called it Babic's constitution. And in this part that relates to the responsibilities of the president, only Babic's picture was missing. In my own exercise of the duties of president, I did not want the duties and powers of the president of the republic to be so great." You continued: "As for your question, especially as far as military aspects are concerned, I understood my position as president of the republic in a very realistic way in the sense that I was aware of my lack of knowledge and experience." And you continued, Mr. Hadzic. You said: "And when you read this point controls armed forces, to me it meant a political function because command required professional skills and I didn't have them."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe there's an intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry about that. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I would suggest if we could see on the screen the original text from the constitution and the translation of this text -- of this article -- particular article. Because as far as I recall, the word "control" was not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We will go to that. It's actually the word that appears in the transcript. I just read the transcript. I don't know whether it's a word that counsel used during his direct examination or whether there's some mistake. But, in any event, we'll clarify it when we get to the text of the constitution, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, the first thing I wanted to point out to you is because you seem to -- you said you understood your position as president in a realistic way, aware of your lack of knowledge and experience, and regarding armed forces it meant a political function because command required professional skills and I didn't have them. The fact that you as a civilian were the head or we'll look at the text, whatever it is in the constitution, Commander-in-Chief, perhaps, of the armed forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I mean, it's not unusual, is it, for a civilian to be -- for a civilian president to be the one ultimately responsible for the armed forces of his country?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I know that under the constitution, the issue at hand was command and control. That was the formulation in the constitution. I had no right to command, and I made inquiries with experts to find out what the distinction was and I didn't know until then what the distinction was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What civilian presidents do is to listen to the advice of their military commanders, make decisions, and otherwise exercise the duties and the responsibilities that they have under the constitution in respect of the armed forces. And that's what you did, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the Supreme Defence Council equal to all the other members and we made decisions jointly. At that time we were under attack from the Croatian side, and we only made reactive decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just indicate that we strongly object to the translation of the term B/C/S term "rukovodjenje" as "the control."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have L3, which is the RSK constitution. And I'll have the tab number in just a moment, Mr. President. It's tab number 382. And we will go straight to Article 78, which is page 22, starts on page 22 of the English version. Article 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because this sets out the powers of the president of the republic, Mr. Hadzic, and I'm going to suggest that, in fact, you exercised these powers without reservation during the time that you were president of the republic. Under the constitution, Mr. Hadzic, first of all, you could nominate candidates for the government members, as it says here, having heard the opinion of the assembly. Item 2, you could nominate to the assembly a candidate for the presiding judge and judges of the constitutional court. You could, number 3, enact -- under item 3, enact laws by decree. And we know that you did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Tab 443, L45. Tab 443, if I misspoke. L45. Now if we can blow up the B/C/S version because I want to correct this transcript or this translation I should say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is law number 66, Mr. Hadzic. Do you see this is the Law on Measures in the Event of a State of Emergency?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in the original language version we actually see this is being done pursuant to Article 78, item 3, of the constitution; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because that actually is not included in the English translation, Mr. President, and so we're going to be requesting the translation be corrected. So this is just one example, Mr. Hadzic, of your -- well, we could go to the end. And can we agree that this law was enacted with your approval or pursuant to your authorities under Article 78, item 3 of the RSK constitution?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, only we should add here with my formal approval. Because whatever was brought to me, I would sign. I did not discuss it, and I didn't understand much about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it was brought to you because in order for it to become law, it had to be signed by you, didn't it? I mean, that's what item number 3 is all about.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said that I formally signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, moving back to the constitution, L3, item number 4 of Article 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Tab 382.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We know that you did carry out duties regarding relations of the Republic of Serbian Krajina with other countries and international organisations in accordance with the law. And we don't need to go into any real detail with that, Mr. Hadzic. Because, for example, all of your dealings, negotiations with internationals, such as Mr. Ahrens, would have been pursuant to this provision; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct. I think, to the best of my recollection, that was the main provision that I dealt with when I was president, representative role and talks with people from the international community and such affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then if we could have, please, tab 542, P2046.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You, in your capacity as president of the RSK, you would come back from these negotiations and you would brief members of the RSK government or its assembly on developments and the discussions that were taking place. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was perhaps at 50 of those meetings, and two or three times maybe at government sessions. That happened a couple of times. But if I said yes to your questions, I would be lying. Sometimes I did it, but mostly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I pulled up these minutes, Mr. Hadzic, because it goes to something you said on your direct examination. Your counsel asked you -- he said: "You also said the most acceptable option is the one involving special status. Were those your words?" And your testimony at transcript page 9719 was: "Yes, those were my words. We, and we in Slavonia, Baranja, were prepared to discuss a special status but certain preconditions had to be met, and it couldn't happen overnight." And what we see in item 1 of the agenda here, Mr. Hadzic, is, in fact, you address certain rumours that certain members of the government were considering some kind of a so-called special status for the RSK, and according to the minutes, you asked the following question on behalf of the RSK and requested an answer: "Are any of the members of the government in attendance in favour of a so-called special status for the RSK in Croatia, and if they are, they should immediately leave the session." So the fact is that you were opposed to special status, despite what you may have claimed in this courtroom, as well as to Mr. Ahrens in your discussions with him. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. And you conflated two things. The special status was discussed in 1991, when I was representative of SAO Slavonia Baranja, et cetera, and that's how I discussed it. And here I said that no representative of Krajina can negotiate single-handedly without consulting the others, and nobody had the right to discussion special status without consulting the parliament and the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Or you. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I. But if I discussed it, I would first have to get approval from the assembly, because it's the assembly that elected me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, we have the -- there's a series of documents, decrees, that you issued around the 22nd of January, 1993 following the Croatia armed forces operation at Maslenica.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Maybe we don't need to go into the documents. Can we agree that you issued a declaration of a state of war throughout the territory of the RSK on the 22nd of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 1458. And this -- maybe -- it may be necessary for private session. This is a FBIS document that is -- I'm not sure that it's redacted yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please. And can we have a tab number, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And here Mr. Dzuro is reading you the passage that I just directed you to: "The Croats had not a single civilian casualty because the Republika Srpska army did not fire on civilian targets ..." And then you go -- and then moving down a few lines, Mr. Dzuro asks you: "Can you tell how did you get this information -- where did you get the information from the -- about the atrocities that the Croats committed there?" And you said: "I received it from the military intelligence service of my -- my military intelligence service of the Republic of Serb Krajina." Now when you just said a moment ago that you didn't have any special service that could verify that information, Mr. Hadzic, that wasn't true. As president of the republic, you did have, in fact, at your disposal military intelligence service, or a military intelligence service, that kept you abreast of those sorts of developments. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was translated or what the understanding of the language was. I said that I received my information from military officers. I said clearly: Military officers. Mile Novkovic was the one who contacted me, and he received that information from the intelligence service, because I, as president of the republic, did not have a special separate intelligence service that some presidents in modern democracies have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 701, P84.50. I apologise. Actually, let me move back to one, tab 680. Tab 680, P46.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, while that's coming up, there have been a fair number of discussions we've had about these District Councils; for example, the District Council SBWS. The one that Mr. Ilic was running in Eastern Slavonia you said was operated independently. I'm going to challenge you on that. I'm going to put to you that when you were the RSK government saw that a district or a region council was acting contrary to policy, you had the power under the RSK constitution to deal with that, and what we see here in this document is your rather swiftly dealing with Mr. Dzakula and his regional councils having entered into that Daruvar agreement with the Croatian authorities. Do you remember this, when you disbanded Mr. Dzakula's regional council for Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that perfectly, but it was not quickly, as you say. The assembly discussed it. And then the government debated it. And then we received information that they had done something on their own initiative and completely bypassing the policy adopted by their own assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if we could zero in -- or I should say scroll in on the top portion of the B/C/S version of the document, just to make it clear. Actually, we need all the text across the top. That's good. Just to make it clear, Mr. Hadzic, because it's not so clear in the translation, when you disbanded this regional council, you were doing it pursuant to Article 78 of the RSK constitution. Isn't that true? You were exercising your presidential powers in disbanding the regional council.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's 28 April. I'm not sure whether the state of the war was still prevailing. But it's in keeping with Article -- the article of the constitution indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'm going to -- this -- the English -- well, it indicates item 8. Item 8 we haven't talked about it, but I'm going to move on it's in the constitution. We can always read it. Item 8, regarding that the president may, on the government's proposal, when a part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina's territory, et cetera, are endangered he announces the state of emergency and adopts acts for taking necessary measures according to circumstances and according to the constitution and law. So you disbanded the Western Slavonia regional council pursuant to item 8 of Article 78, which then brings us to the last document for the day. Tab 701, P84.50. Mr. Hadzic, this is - and I'm going to go quickly because we're running out of time today - an interview with Goran Hadzic in "Borba," a Belgrade publication, 24/25 July 1993. And I want to bring you back to this, in part, based on what you said on the third page of the English. That is R33.0576 is the ERN number. And here you are referring to -- I should say, just slightly below the halfway mark of the page, you were asked: "You have broken with some close associates. Why?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I don't know if we can blow up the text to make it readable for you. It may be, Mr. President - I think I've got a little bit of time remaining on Monday - we're best just to leave this till then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is it for the day, and for the weekend, and so we will be back on Monday at 9.00, and you're still on your oath, and you know what the consequences thereof are. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 1st day of September, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.00 p.m.,
